name: Antiphanes of Macedonia
bio: Antiphanes of Macedonia is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to Augustan age. Paton's index lists the poet among the writers of the Wreath of Philippus, the Garland compiled in the first century AD.
This archive carries the 5 epigrams ascribed to the poet in the third volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book IX: 84, 245, 256, 258, 409).

poems.title: Book IX, 84
poems.author: Antiphanes of Macedonia
poems.text: A shepherd saw the straying hull of a sea-tost boat carried along shore by the fierce waves. He seized it with his hand, and it dragged its saviour into the deep sea, so bitter was its hatred of all mankind. Thus the shepherd met with the fate of a shipwrecked mariner. Alas! both the woods and the harbour are put in mourning by that boat.

poems.title: Book IX, 245
poems.author: Antiphanes of Macedonia
poems.text: By the unhappy marriage-bed of Petale at her bitter bridal stood Hades, not Hymen. For, as she fled alone through the darkness, dreading the first taste of the yoke of Cypris—a terror common to all maidens—the cruel watch-dogs killed her. We had hoped to see her a wife and suddenly we could hardly find her corpse.

poems.title: Book IX, 256
poems.author: Antiphanes of Macedonia
poems.text: I rnoucur that half of me was still alive, and that half produced one single apple on the highest branch. But the brute that ravages fruit-trees, the hairy-backed caterpillar, envied me even the one, and ate it up. Envy’s eyes are set on great wealth, but the creature who lays waste a little substance I must call worse even than Envy’s self.

poems.title: Book IX, 258
poems.author: Antiphanes of Macedonia
poems.text: I who once gushed with abundance of sweet water, have now lost my nymphs even to the last drop. For the murderer washed his bloody hands in my water, and tainted it with the stain. Ever since the maidens have retired from the sunlight, exclaiming, “We nymphs mix with Bacchus alone, not with Ares.”

poems.title: Book IX, 409
poems.author: Antiphanes of Macedonia
poems.text: If there be one who does not take delight in the strains of the flute and the sweet sound of harp-playing, or in nectareous wine, oldest of the old, or in torches, revels, garlands, and scent, but who takes a frugal supper and stores up with greedy hands the fruits of stealthy-footed usury, to me he is dead, and I pass by the... corpse, who hoards for the weasands of others.

poems.title: Book X, 100
poems.author: Antiphanes of Macedonia
poems.text: Brief would be the whole span of life that we wretched men live, even if grey old age awaited us all, and briefer yet is the space of our prime. Therefore, while the season is ours, let all be in plenty, song, love, carousal. Henceforth is the winter of heavy eld. Thou wouldst give ten minae to be a man, but no such fetters shall be set on thy manhood.

poems.title: Book XI, 168
poems.author: Antiphanes of Macedonia
poems.text: Thou reckonest up thy money, poor wretch ; but Time, just as it breeds interest, so, as it overtakes thee, gives birth to grey old age. And so having neither drunk wine, nor bound thy temples with flowers, having never known sweet ointment or a delicate little love, thou shalt die, leaving a great and wealthy testament, and of all thy riches carrying away with thee but one obol.

poems.title: Book XI, 322
poems.author: Antiphanes of Macedonia
poems.text: Idly curious race of grammarians, ye who dig up by the roots the poetry of others; unhappy book-worms that walk on thorns, defilers of the great, proud of your Erinna, bitter and dry dogs set on by Callimachus, bane of poets, darkness to little beginners, away with you, bugs that secretly bite the eloquent.

poems.title: Book XI, 348
poems.author: Antiphanes of Macedonia
poems.text: O parricide, man more savage than the beasts, all things hate thee, everywhere thy fate awaits thee. If thou fliest on the land, the wolf is near; and if thou climbest high on trees, the asp on the branches is a terror. Thou makest trial of the Nile, too, but he nourishes in his eddies the crocodile, a brute most just to the impious.

poems.title: Vain Riches (Mackail)
poems.author: Antiphanes of Macedonia
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Thou reckonest, poor wretch; but advancing time breeds white old age even as it does interest; and neither having drunk, nor bound a flower on thy brows, nor ever known myrrh nor a delicate darling, thou shalt be dead, leaving thy great treasury in its wealth, out of those many coins carrying with thee but the one.
